correctness.rationale: The common-neighbor definition on the bipartite incidence graph forbids mixed-side simplices. Point-side maximal simplices are block point-sets, and block-side maximal simplices are the stars of individual points. The Steiner condition makes any two distinct maximal simplices on a given side meet in at most one vertex; thus each simplex independently collapses onto an arbitrary spanning tree without touching shared vertices. On the point side the resulting connected graph has v vertices and b(k−1) edges, giving rank b(k−1)−v+1. On the block side it has b vertices and v(r−1) edges; unique point-pair blocks connect arbitrary two blocks via a short path, so rank v(r−1)−b+1. The incidence equality bk=vr identifies these with μ. For PG(2,q), v=b=q²+q+1, k=r=q+1, giving μ=q³. Independently reconstructed the Fano incidence graph (q=2), verifying both graph ranks eight; other finite examples in source serve only as corroboration. The relative simplex-to-tree collapse can be proved by coning an inductive collapse on a leaf deletion; no extension claim is based solely on examples.

originality.rationale: Kozlov proves the general simple-homotopy equivalence of N(G) and Hom(K2,G), without computing this design-incidence family. Shukla gives only qualitative wedge-of-circles for maximum degree at most three; Steiner designs include arbitrarily high degrees and the exact μ formula is missing. A published scale-two Vietoris–Rips projective-plane statement concerns a distinct simplex predicate and dimension (two-spheres rather than neighborhood-circle wedges). A general linear-hypergraph clique-union collapse may subsume the proof; this is disclosed as the strongest residual alias risk.

value.rationale: Steiner designs and their incidence graphs are canonical families in combinatorial design theory. The theorem gives an exact simple-homotopy classification for both dual components in all admissible parameters, with natural cycle rank equal to the incidence graph’s first Betti number; μ=q³ gives a clean projective-plane invariant. This is an explicit and reusable structural calculation rather than an isolated test instance.

final_claim: For every nontrivial Steiner S(2,k,v), the ordinary Lovász neighborhood complex of its point-block incidence graph has two components, each simplicially collapsible to a graph of cycle rank μ=vr-v-b+1; for a projective plane of order q, μ=q^3.
limitations: An older result phrased as linear-hypergraph nerve or graph of cliques might yield the same simple collapse and exact rank; no exhaustive literature proof of priority.
